data.title: Confronting the Homelessness Crisis Through Art
data.summary: Made possible by an Arts for Social Justice Grant from SCU’s College of Arts & Sciences and additional funding from Destination: Home SV, the Unhoused Initiative at Santa Clara University is proud to present “Confronting the Homelessness Crisis through Art” - a fall quarter art exhibition highlighting artistic works of people with lived experience of homelessness. Through the project, we hope to shine a light on the homelessness crisis in Silicon Valley through creative mediums and their creators. Visual art, poetry, music and presentations, will center the perspectives of people who have experienced homelessness during this four-week exhibition.
data.description:
An exhibition of visual art created by people with lived experience of homelessness will be on-display on the 2nd floor of the University Library from October 26th to November 20th, 2026. Pieces include paintings and photography. Our artists include Amanda Cole, John Betts, Liat Noten, Gabriella Gabrian and Nadine Zellner.

The exhibit is part of a larger project showcasing the homelessness crisis through art and artists’ viewpoints. All events are on campus, free of charge and open to all.

Additional Events:

  • October 29th and 30th: a display of the Memorial Tombstones for the Unhoused on the lawn between Kenna & Benson
  • October 29th, 11:30am: a guided reflection at the Tombstone Display, led by Tony Cortese of the Ignatian Center
  • October 30th, 4:30pm: a performance by musician, Shamira Dickerson, at the Tombstone Display
  • November 9th, 4:30pm: an artists’ talk & reception featuring Art Hazelwood and other artists participating in the larger project.

This group exhibition draws parallels from artists in Hokkaido, Japan and select faculty members from the Santa Clara University Department of Art and Art History. The exhibit reflects the thirty-five-year relationship between SCU and artists from Hokkaido, and compares and contrasts work from both groups to show the similarity and differences in which the artists approach a variety of mediums.

data.title: IN-PERSON ONLY: The Mythological Mayhem of Ovid’s Metamorphoses
data.description:
Monday, October 19, 26, November 2, 9, and 16
10:00 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

THIS COURSE WILL BE RECORDED.

Register Here

It is one of the delightful ironies of Western culture that the best and most influential narrator of Greek myths was a Roman writing in Latin many centuries after the height of Greek creativity. Ovid was the author of The Metamorphoses, an epic collection of over 250 myths, mostly Greek. We will examine select tales that are especially representative of Ovid’s accomplishment as a storyteller: his wit, his clever manipulation of inherited tales, his not-infrequent profundity, his influence, and his subversiveness. This is your chance to meet—or become reacquainted with—many of the most influential Greco-Roman mythical figures. There are the gods, of course: the henpecked and ever-concupiscent Jove, broken-hearted Apollo, pathologically virginal Diana, cuckolded Vulcan. However, it is often the mortals who have inspired authors, artists, and philosophers over the past two millennia: Narcissus, Pygmalion, Pyramus and Thisbe (models for Romeo and Juliet), Daphne, Orpheus and Eurydice, Europa, Midas (the golden-touch version, not the muffler), to name just a few. The epic has it all: lots of love stories (almost all of which end horribly), women turning into men, men turning into women, statues turning into women, just about everyone turning into animals, and women turning into all sorts of vegetation in order to escape a god’s attention.

John Heath received his B.A. from Pomona College, his M.A. and Ph.D. from Stanford University. In 1989, he was given an American Philological Association Excellence in Teaching Award. He has been awarded the Phi Beta Kappa Society (Northern California) teaching award for excellence in undergraduate education, an Arnold L. and Lois S. Graves Award for his contributions to undergraduate teaching in the humanities, and the Brutocao Award for Teaching Excellence. He teaches all levels of Greek and Latin, as well as courses on classical literature in translation, Greek mythology, and Greek and Roman culture. He has published thirty articles on Latin and Greek literature. With Victor Davis Hanson, he wrote the notorious Who Killed Homer? The Demise of Classical Education and the Recovery of Greek Wisdom (Free Press, 1998), as well as Bonfire of the Humanities: Rescuing Classics from an Impoverished Age (ICS 2001, co-authored with Bruce Thornton). In 2005, Cambridge University Press published The Talking Greeks: Speech, Animals, and the Other in Homer, Aeschylus, and Plato. His latest book, Yahweh or Zeus? Why We Would Be Better Off with Homer’s Gods, was published by Routledge in 2019. Professor Heath lives in Santa Cruz with his wife, Lisa, and younger daughter, Alexis. This is his third course for OLLI@SCU.

data.title: IN-PERSON ONLY: The History and Design of American Gardens: For Food and Medicine, For Beauty and Prestige
data.description:
Monday, November 2, 9, and 16
1:00 p.m. - 3:00 p.m.

THIS COURSE WILL BE RECORDED.

Register Here

In a variety of ways, gardens have been a significant part of our country’s history since its very beginning. The first thing the English colonists did was to plant the seeds they had providentially brought with them, both for food (kitchen gardens) and for medicine (“physic” or botanical gardens). When those seeds failed, they learned techniques from friendly Native Americans with extensive experience gardening in the East Coast climate. Later, in the eighteenth century, estate gardens were planted for beauty and prestige (pleasure gardens). George Washington and Thomas Jefferson were both avid gardeners and planned gardens on their own estates, introducing European garden tastes into American gardens. They brought gardeners to the White House, where impressive gardens were planned. The taste for impressive and prestigious gardens continued into the 19th and 20th centuries, as prosperous families across the country from the East Coast to California oversaw the design of their large estate gardens. Some of those gardens were designed by great women gardeners such as Beatrix Farrand, Bunny Mellon, Florence Yoch, and Marion Coffin. Garden design in the 20th century changed in step with changes in the arts, especially painting and product design. Designers like Thomas Church, who designed many gardens in California, including in the Bay Area, adapted the abstract shapes of modern designers to the outlines of, for example, swimming pools.

Christy Junkerman earned her Ph.D. in Art History from the University of California, Berkeley, and her B.A. (in English) from the University of Wisconsin, Madison. Her specialty is Italian Renaissance art, though her M.A. (also from Berkeley) was in French medieval architecture. She has lived and studied in Aix-en-Provence in southern France and in Venice. During the year in Venice on a fellowship, she worked on her dissertation on the image of courtesans in early 16th-century Venetian painting. She taught several courses at UC Berkeley and Stanford before accepting a position in the Department of Art and Art History at San Jose State. Her teaching at San Jose State centered on a series of courses and seminars in Italian Renaissance art, but also included surveys of the whole span of Western art. She developed an interest in the Arts and Crafts Movement and its relevance to the department’s history, and taught seminars that connected the two subjects. She helped the Art History students mount an exhibition of works in the department’s collection. She has taught many Continuing Studies courses at Stanford. She has also led many trips to Italy for Stanford Travel/Study, including walking trips, family trips, and even a bicycle trip. She has lectured several times for the Fine Arts Museums in San Francisco. This is her sixth course for OLLI.

data.title: Global Learning Application Filing Period
data.summary:
Undergraduate Students

Summer 2027, Fall 2027, and Winter/Spring 2028 programs

The application filing period for the following academic year abroad runs from mid-November to early December. Applications may be submitted at any time during this filing period. Applications receive a time stamp with the date and time of submission, placing them in numerical order. Once the filing period closes, applications are reviewed. This review takes place from December through late January, and program nominations are made based on the time stamp of submission after applications have been evaluated to determine applicants meet program requirements. Following evaluation, students are notified of their application status by early February.
